nodes.label: Booking & Appointment Management System
nodes.author: AmmarDw
nodes.rationale: MVP chosen from the AI bootcamp's suggested-projects list (#1). Monorepo: app/backend Spring Boot + app/frontend Next.js, docs at project root. Real build compressed to ~2 days while docs narrate the official 6-day agenda.

nodes.label: Conversation History Protocol
nodes.rationale: conversation_history.md is the single source of truth and persistent project memory that survives context-window limits, session resets and model switches. Chat stays a minimal pointer; the LLM reformats raw prompts to clean Markdown without removing content and writes structured '§ N — Response to Prompt #M' sections. Append-only: historical entries are never retro-renumbered because they record what was true when written.

nodes.label: PROJECT_REPORT.md (graded deliverable)
nodes.rationale: Single graded report. Per section: brief instructions → template → short generic example → the actual booking-system data. Deliberately kept below capstone depth because the bootcamp audience is beginner–intermediate.

nodes.label: implementation_plan.md
nodes.rationale: Granular coding plan: architecture decisions + milestones M0–M8 with file paths, endpoints, per-milestone acceptance criteria, a 'Manual steps (you do these)' table, and [You]/[Claude] tags so the human's physical steps are explicit.

nodes.label: research_plan.md (spikes R1–R4)
nodes.rationale: Registered four research spikes that were prerequisites for Day 2: R1 Google Meet feasibility/cost, R2 dashboard patterns, R3 landing-page sections, R4 calendar UX (popup vs dedicated page).

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md (project memory)
nodes.rationale: Holds both documentation conventions (part A) and booking-system domain logic (part B). Accumulated every gotcha discovered during the build so the same class of bug can't hide again.

nodes.label: AI_MVP_Bootcamp_6_Days_AR.pdf
nodes.rationale: Source spec: 6 days / 36 hours, teams of 2–3, 3–5 core features, demo data only, daily rhythm 1h concepts + 1h live + 3h build + 1h review. Evaluation weights 20/30/25/15/10. Audience = non-experts, which drives the lightweight-documentation stance.

nodes.label: common_blueprints.md (RBAC + Landing Page standards)
nodes.rationale: Trainer's private blueprint file cited for §1 RBAC baseline and §2 Landing Page Standard; explicitly not shared with trainees.

nodes.label: SpeedIt Capstone Report (style reference only)
nodes.author: Ammar
nodes.rationale: Used only as a professionalism/style reference. Explicitly must NOT be matched in depth or technicality — the bootcamp audience would be lost.

nodes.label: bootcamp-mvp-process.md (process rule file)
nodes.rationale: Project-agnostic guide steering Claude across the bootcamp days. Later reduced to a lean 'operating contract' (§1 golden rules and §4 standing instructions deleted) once duplication with the package CLAUDE.md was flagged.

nodes.label: requirements-standards.md (EARS + Gherkin standard)
nodes.rationale: Global rule: EARS syntax, flat IDs (FR-n/NFR-n), user stories, Gherkin acceptance criteria, Necessary/Atomic/Verifiable/Clear check. Later deleted as an always-loaded rule in the trainee package and converted into the writing-requirements skill to cut per-message context cost.

nodes.label: i18n-directionality.md (RTL/LTR rule)
nodes.rationale: Created in Phase 0 as an improved, context7-verified successor to the legacy i18n_context_system.md blueprint. In the trainee package it is paths:-scoped so it only loads on UI files; worst case degrades to today's always-loaded behaviour, which is why the (buggy) paths: mechanism was acceptable here but not as the primary lazy-loading mechanism.

nodes.label: git-commit-attribution.md rule
nodes.rationale: Added to the trainee package so trainees don't hit the 'Claude added itself as a Co-Authored-By' problem the trainer had personally hit. The specific incident (repo, commit hashes, date) was generalized rather than reproduced, since it belongs to the trainer's own history.

nodes.label: Single User entity with role field
nodes.rationale: Dropped the separate Provider entity: one User with role CONSUMER/PROVIDER/ADMIN 'will cut it'. Availability binds to a User with role=PROVIDER; a UserService N:M records which services a provider offers. Simpler model, and it lets a provider act as a consumer elsewhere without a second identity.

nodes.label: Availability bound to provider, not service (FR-4)
nodes.rationale: A provider has 5 real time slots in a day, so offering '1 appointment per service × 5 services' is bad UX and would misrepresent capacity. Binding slots to the provider means booking one slot marks it reserved across every service that provider offers — 5 slots shown per service, not 25 bookable appointments. Proven by curl: rebooking the same slot under a different service still returns 409.

nodes.label: AvailabilitySlot entity
nodes.rationale: Owns SlotStatus (AVAILABLE/BOOKED) and mirrors the uq_provider_slot unique constraint that enforces FR-4's one-slot-per-provider rule at the DB level.

nodes.label: Booking entity + BookingService
nodes.rationale: POST /api/bookings is @Transactional, validates slot AVAILABLE + within the booking window + that the provider actually offers the requested service, then flips the slot to BOOKED and creates the Booking.

nodes.label: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE slot row lock
nodes.rationale: findByIdForUpdate pessimistically row-locks the availability slot inside the booking transaction so two concurrent consumers can't both take the same slot — the double-booking race is closed in the DB, not in application logic.

nodes.label: UserService N:M (provider ↔ services)
nodes.rationale: Modelled as a plain JPA @ManyToMany — no separate junction entity was needed since the join table carries no extra columns.

nodes.label: AppSettings single-row table
nodes.rationale: Chosen over both pure-yaml and a generic key/value table. Pure yaml can't hold a runtime admin setting: it is read once at startup, is packaged inside the JAR on read-only/ephemeral prod filesystems, and writing YAML from app code risks corruption. So the default lives in application.yaml (booking.max-horizon-months: 6, @ConfigurationProperties) while the admin's live value persists in one typed row, seeded from the default, cached in memory and refreshed on update.

nodes.label: SystemSetting generic key/value table (superseded)
nodes.rationale: Initial design for storing the booking horizon. Rejected as over-engineered for a single value once the user pointed out that adding a whole table for one setting is inefficient and no second key/value pair was foreseeable.

nodes.label: Admin-configurable booking horizon
nodes.rationale: Admin sets a max booking duration (default 6 months); consumers cannot book beyond today+horizon and past dates are non-selectable and non-navigable. Calendar navigation adapts: the year picker lists only the 1–2 years the window spans, and the 12-month grid shadows months before the current month or beyond the horizon. Enforced in BOTH the calendar UI and server-side booking validation — the client is never trusted.

nodes.label: Provider advance limit = ceil(horizon × 1.5)
nodes.rationale: Two windows instead of one: consumers book within 1× horizon, providers may pre-load availability up to ceil(horizon × multiplier) — the user's +50% option (6 → 9 months) chosen for simplicity over doubling. The multiplier is yaml-only and NOT admin-facing so no extra user-facing setting appears. The window is rolling, so pre-loaded slots become bookable as time advances.

nodes.label: Pressure-coloured calendar with available/total counts
nodes.rationale: Each day shows available/total (e.g. 3/8); colour and opacity convey booking pressure — High ≥4 (green/light), Medium =3 (yellow), Low 1–2 (warm/alert), none = shadowed. Colours are derived from the site palette so they don't disrupt it, and are reinforced by the number badge + opacity to stay colourblind-safe. Weekends are deliberately NOT special: shadowing is driven purely by slot availability, because a provider may choose to work Fri/Sat as a part-time job.

nodes.label: Stacked provider dropdowns (slot display option 2)
nodes.rationale: Chosen over admin-defined unified time slots and over a flat stacked list. Each provider is a dropdown; expanding shows that provider's slots for the date, and multiple dropdowns can be open at once to compare. Scales by scrolling as providers grow, and preserves provider-preferred (possibly overlapping) times rather than forcing everyone onto a discrete admin grid.

nodes.label: Dedicated /book/[serviceId] calendar page (R4)
nodes.rationale: Research R4 resolved 'modal vs page' in favour of a dedicated page: it is a multi-step flow, it yields a shareable URL, and it makes the sign-in redirect-back flow clean.

nodes.label: Shared provider/admin dashboard (/dashboard)
nodes.rationale: One UI for both roles rather than two dashboards; admins simply get extra capability (a provider selector/filter, all-data scope). Providers see only their own data plus any bookings they made themselves as a consumer. Rebuilt in the M6.3 fidelity pass into filter bar + 4 range-driven stat cards + SVG chart + 42-cell calendar + list.

nodes.label: GET /api/bookings/{feed,stats,chart}
nodes.rationale: Three endpoints backing the rebuilt dashboard, all taking comma-separated serviceIds/statuses/providerIds plus from/to. Stat cards are date-range-driven and narrowed by service+provider but deliberately NOT by the status filter, because each card has an intrinsic status meaning (a no-show rate needs completed+no_show regardless of the filter). feed returns real bookings plus synthesized VACANT entries for open slots using a negative id (=-slotId) and null consumer.

nodes.label: /appointments 'My Appointments' (consumer-only)
nodes.rationale: Briefly opened to every role in §69, then explicitly reverted: providers/admins must not see this page at all (nav link hidden, direct navigation redirects to /dashboard). Their own consumer-side bookings surface only through the '(You)' merge into the dashboard, so the same data is never duplicated across two pages. Backed by GET /api/bookings?mine=true, hard-scoped server-side so a providerId filter param cannot escape the caller's own scope.

nodes.label: Shared AppointmentDetailsModal
nodes.rationale: One details view wired into BOTH the consumer /appointments table and the provider/admin /dashboard table via row click, rather than two near-duplicate modals. It is the only place the meeting link is shown — the table row itself deliberately does not carry it. Later gained the role/time-gated status-transition buttons.

nodes.label: LoadingOverlay (blurred full-page wait)
nodes.rationale: The Book button triggers a synchronous Google Calendar + email round-trip server-side that is slow enough to feel broken. A full-page blur + spinner covers the wait with the content staying visible underneath (never disappearing), per the explicit spec. Verified mid-request under network throttling.

nodes.label: '(You)' marking for self-booked rows
nodes.rationale: A clarifying question was asked before implementing: '(You)' only makes sense where the consumer field varies row-to-row, which the dedicated My-Appointments page never can. So the marking lives on the merged provider/admin dashboard, where a bold + primary-teal name with a trailing '(You)' distinguishes the viewer's own patient-role booking from real patient rows.

nodes.label: Provider cannot book their own availability
nodes.rationale: Enforced twice: the signed-in provider's own entry is filtered out of the day-view list client-side, AND BookingService rejects it with 400 before any DB write. The client-side filter alone is not trusted. A provider booking a DIFFERENT provider's service as a consumer stays allowed. This rule was never inferred by the assistant — it only appeared after the trainer explicitly noticed and demanded it, which later became the curriculum's canonical example of why human review surfaces implicit logical rules.

nodes.label: BookingStatus lifecycle (5 statuses)
nodes.rationale: CONFIRMED (initial) → one terminal state. CANCELLED by the consumer only >24h before start and frees the slot back to AVAILABLE; COMPLETED and NO_SHOW are gated on the slot's END time (user's explicit choice over start time); NO_SHOW leaves the slot BOOKED. VACANT is never persisted — a dashboard-only synthesized label for open slots, deliberately excluded from the V7 CHECK constraint so it cannot be written even though it is a Java enum value. Cancel-frees-slot vs no-show-doesn't is moot in practice since no-show only applies to past slots that can't be rebooked.

nodes.label: Public landing page (R3 section list)
nodes.rationale: Hero → How-it-works/journey → Services preview → optional FAQ → Footer. Social proof is deliberately excluded: 'we are talking about an MVP, so having a social-proof section is not logically correct'. The services preview is server-fetched live.

nodes.label: Admin-managed provider onboarding (FR-16)
nodes.rationale: Public sign-up creates CONSUMER only; the admin creates providers or promotes a consumer→provider. Chosen over a role picker at sign-up for vetting and consistency with the admin-controlled services/assignment model. Enforced server-side: a crafted register body requesting role ADMIN still yields CONSUMER (privilege-escalation guard verified by curl).

nodes.label: Bulk availability generator
nodes.rationale: Weekdays × date range × time ranges. Available to providers (own slots) AND admins (any provider) — corrected from an initial admin-only design. Bounded by the provider advance limit, idempotent (re-runs skip existing slots), and deliberately NON-destructive: the Claude Design copy said 'conflicts will be replaced', which was rejected because overwriting could delete already-booked slots.

nodes.label: diagrams/consumer_booking_activity.drawio
nodes.rationale: Activity diagram with two swimlanes — Consumer (blue) and System (green, treated as a stakeholder) — plus an orange decision node. The 'timeline per stakeholder' idea was kept deliberately simple to avoid overcomplicating the diagram.

nodes.label: diagrams/erd.drawio
nodes.rationale: 8 entities drawn from the LIVE Flyway schema (V1__init_schema.sql) rather than re-derived from the report's prose, so the diagram matches what actually runs. Teal headers matching the design system, PK/FK/UQ column annotations, plain 1—N / 1—0..1 cardinality labels. A first pass that produced empty entity boxes was caught and rewritten before finalizing.

nodes.label: Google Meet links via Google Calendar API (R1)
nodes.rationale: Feasible on a FREE Gmail account via Calendar API events.insert with conferenceDataVersion=1 and conferenceData.createRequest (hangoutsMeet) under user OAuth2 — the 'Workspace only' belief applies to the Admin-SDK path, not user OAuth. Custom UI is fully preserved because the result is just a hangoutLink string. GoogleCalendarService never throws: it returns null on any failure so a Meet outage can never fail a booking (NFR-4).

nodes.label: Per-provider Google account connection
nodes.rationale: Adopted from the start over a single shared host account. Technically one host would work (invited guests are 'Trusted' and join without an admit while the waiting room is off), but the one-host model puts every meeting on an absent operator's calendar and makes them the only person who could clear any edge case. Per-provider means the provider is organizer AND actually attends. Scope calendar.events plus userinfo.email (added beyond the original spec so the connect page can show WHICH Google account is linked); refresh token stored encrypted; prompt=consent forces a refresh token even on reconnect.

nodes.label: GoogleAccountConnection entity
nodes.rationale: Fields: userId, googleEmail, refreshTokenEnc, scope, connectedAt, nullable fallbackMeetUrl. The nullable fallback column is what lets a provider be bookable without ever completing OAuth.

nodes.label: Fallback persistent Meet link
nodes.rationale: A provider who skips OAuth can paste a persistent personal Meet link instead. A provider with NEITHER is not bookable — BookingService rejects with 400 before any DB write (FR-13). Resolution order at booking time: Google Calendar first, fallback link if not connected or if generation failed. V6 seeded the demo providers with fallback links precisely so the new gate wouldn't regress the already-verified M4 booking flow.

nodes.label: OAuth state as a short-lived signed JWT
nodes.rationale: Google's OAuth callback is a plain browser redirect carrying no Authorization header, so the JWT filter cannot identify which provider is returning. JwtService#generateOAuthState/parseOAuthState carries the initiating provider's user id in a 10-minute, purpose-tagged token signed with the existing JWT key — the only way a public callback endpoint can know whose connection it is completing.

nodes.label: TokenCipher (AES-256-GCM refresh-token encryption)
nodes.rationale: Key derived as SHA-256(TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY) so any non-empty configured string yields a valid 256-bit key — removes a whole class of 'invalid key length' configuration failures.

nodes.label: Gotcha: OAuth callback params must be optional
nodes.rationale: Google's most common non-happy path — the provider clicking Cancel on the consent screen — redirects back with error=access_denied and NO code param at all. Declaring code/state as required @RequestParams turned that into an uncaught MissingServletRequestParameterException and a raw 500 page. Fixed by making both optional and checking for a Google-supplied error before touching the token exchange. Found by deliberately curling that exact shape, not by review.

nodes.label: EmailService (Gmail SMTP confirmations)
nodes.rationale: Gmail SMTP on port 465 (implicit SSL, NOT STARTTLS) with an app password. Two emails are sent on every booking: the consumer confirmation (service, date, time, meeting link, plus the provider's name and email) and a separate provider notification (naming the consumer's name and email) so the provider learns of a new appointment without checking the dashboard. Never throws — an email failure can never fail a booking (NFR-4).

nodes.label: Gotcha: spring.mail nested properties need bracket-quoted YAML keys
nodes.rationale: Keys under spring.mail.properties must be written as "[mail.smtp.ssl.enable]": true, not as nested YAML maps. Paired with the Gmail-465-is-implicit-SSL fact: ssl.enable matters, starttls.enable does not.

nodes.label: Spring Boot 4.1.0 backend (app/backend)
nodes.rationale: Docs originally said 'Spring Boot 3'; the actual Initializr output was 4.1.0 with 4.x starter names (spring-boot-starter-webmvc). Reconciled the docs to reality rather than downgrading. Group com.ammar, artifact booking-system, package com.ammar.bookingsystem, Java 21 — chosen over the com.example/demo defaults which are painful to rename later. Feature-based packaging (user, service, availability, booking, google, settings).

nodes.label: Flyway schema migrations (V1–V7)
nodes.rationale: Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate ddl-auto is set to validate so entities are only checked against it. V1 init schema (8 entities, role/status CHECK constraints, uq_provider_slot), V2 seed app_settings, V3 demo services, V4 demo providers+slots, V5 demo admin, V6 provider fallback links, V7 add booking statuses. Demo data only, per the bootcamp rule.

nodes.label: Gotcha: Spring Boot 4 moved FlywayAutoConfiguration to its own module
nodes.rationale: A bare flyway-core + flyway-database-postgresql does NOT trigger autoconfiguration in Boot 4 — it fails SILENTLY: no error, Flyway never runs, the DB stays empty. It went undetected for several turns because no entities existed yet, so ddl-auto:validate had nothing to check. Surfaced only when M1's entities produced 'missing table [app_settings]'; the condition-evaluation report showed zero Flyway mentions. Fix: use org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway and keep flyway-database-postgresql explicit (it is optional inside the starter).

nodes.label: Gotcha: Jackson 3 relocation (tools.jackson.*)
nodes.rationale: This stack's Jackson is tools.jackson.*, not com.fasterxml.jackson.*. Importing the classic ObjectMapper compiles fine but throws NoClassDefFoundError at runtime. Spring MVC's own JSON is unaffected (Boot autoconfigures against whatever Jackson is on the classpath) — only a manual import breaks. Fixed by hand-writing the small fixed-shape JSON for security-layer 401/403 responses instead of depending on Jackson in a low-level filter at all.

nodes.label: Convention: @Component instead of @Service
nodes.rationale: The domain entity is deliberately named Service to match the ERD. Any class importing that entity cannot also import org.springframework.stereotype.Service under its simple name, so business-logic beans uniformly use @Component — this sidesteps the clash everywhere at once instead of fully-qualifying case by case.

nodes.label: Stateless JWT Bearer authentication
nodes.rationale: security/ package: JwtService, JwtAuthenticationFilter, AppUserDetailsService, UserPrincipal, CurrentUser. Chosen with the user as the auth mechanism. BCrypt hashing, method security, stateless sessions. jjwt 0.13.0 API drift was hit — even context7's own indexed snippet (Jwts.parserBuilder()) was stale for that version; the IDE's live diagnostics caught it and it was fixed to Jwts.parser()...parseSignedClaims().

nodes.label: Gotcha: SecurityConfig needs explicit exceptionHandling entry points
nodes.rationale: Without .exceptionHandling(...) an unauthenticated/forbidden request has no AuthenticationEntryPoint and surfaces as an opaque 500 instead of 401/403. Compounded by a bare @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) with NO logging, which silently converted real bugs into 500s. Also: never permitAll the whole /api/auth/** — that accidentally permitted /api/auth/me, letting an anonymous request reach the controller and throw. Fixed by naming /register and /login explicitly, adding NoHandlerFoundException → 404, and adding logging to the generic handler.

nodes.label: Gotcha: @PreAuthorize denials need their own AccessDeniedException handler
nodes.rationale: Method-security AOP throws AccessDeniedException INSIDE the MVC handler invocation, so unlike an unauthenticated request it never reaches SecurityConfig's filter-level accessDeniedHandler — the blanket Exception.class handler catches it first and returns 500 instead of 403. Requires a dedicated @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class) in GlobalExceptionHandler.

nodes.label: Gotcha: void @DeleteMapping returns 200 + empty body, not 204
nodes.rationale: The frontend api() helper only special-cased 204 before calling res.json(), which throws on empty text — so a successful delete surfaced as a UI error even though the row was actually gone. Fixed at BOTH ends: all deletes return ResponseEntity.noContent(), and api() now checks response text before parsing regardless of status so the class of bug cannot recur. Caught via network-request inspection in the browser, not by review.

nodes.label: Gotcha: Hibernate first-level cache + inverse @ManyToMany
nodes.rationale: After mutating the owning side (User.services) and re-fetching the inverse side's owner (Service) in the SAME persistence context, Hibernate returns the already-loaded instance with its previously-materialized, now-stale providers collection — it does not silently refresh. The provider-assignment PUT response showed empty providers while the DB was correct. Fixed by building the response from the already-known new set instead of re-querying. Caught by comparing the immediate response against a follow-up GET.

nodes.label: Native Windows PostgreSQL 16 instead of Docker
nodes.rationale: docker ps showed no containers; port 5432 was already held by an existing native postgresql-x64-16 Windows service. Rather than fight the port conflict, the native service was adopted. DB booking_system owned by user bookingadmin — ownership alone grants public-schema rights on PostgreSQL 15+, so no extra GRANTs were needed (the IDE extension's CREATE USER template only GRANTed on already-existing tables, which would have left the app unable to create anything).

nodes.label: spring-dotenv (.env loading) + working-directory gotcha
nodes.rationale: springboot4-dotenv auto-loads .env as a Spring property source in dev while real environment variables still take precedence — safe in production, no manual shell exports locally. The gotcha: it loads .env from the PROCESS WORKING DIRECTORY. ./mvnw runs from app/backend so it worked, but IntelliJ ran from elsewhere, so DB_PASSWORD was empty → 'SCRAM authentication, no password provided' → the misleading downstream 'Unable to determine Dialect' symptom. Fix: set the IntelliJ run-config working directory to app/backend.

nodes.label: Rule: real secrets in .env, placeholders only in .env.example
nodes.rationale: The real DB password had been placed in .env.example, which is committed — only .env is git-ignored. application.yaml was already correct (${VAR:default} placeholders were fallback defaults, not hardcoded secrets). Confirmed no exposure because the project was not yet a git repo, so there was no history to scrub.

nodes.label: Next.js 16 frontend (app/frontend)
nodes.rationale: create-next-app produced Next.js 16 / React 19 / Tailwind v4 — docs had said 'Next.js 14', reconciled to reality the same way the Spring Boot version was. Nested .git removed to keep the monorepo single-repo. AGENTS.md warns this Next.js has breaking changes vs training data: check node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing page code.

nodes.label: Claude Design → Design System → DesignSync loop
nodes.rationale: Round-trip starting in the 'other' direction: Claude Code writes ready-to-paste Claude Design prompts (a Design-System setup prompt A, then one per screen B–J) already encoding teal tokens, availability-pressure rules, RTL and the relevant FRs. A Design System project is created first — chosen over blank or template starts for cross-screen consistency. Each screen is a SEPARATE generation from the same system so one screen's iteration history doesn't bleed into another. Then DesignSync pulls components into the repo one at a time. Rule discovered: one prompt = one screen (a crammed 'Connect Google + Services mgmt' prompt confused Claude Design about whether to produce one or two screens).

nodes.label: DS component library (src/components/ds)
nodes.rationale: Tokens (availability-pressure + teal + light/dark, Arabic RTL typography swap) plus 11 ES-module components, barrelled at @/components/ds. The 4 Claude Design reference screens are kept as visual reference ONLY because they use Claude Design sandbox globals (window.BookItDesignSystem_*) rather than ES imports. Components were extended backward-compatibly rather than forked: CalendarDayCell gained an optional total prop, Table an onRowClick, Modal a hideActions.

nodes.label: Gotcha: DS component client-boundary (Accordion useState)
nodes.rationale: Accordion.jsx calls React.useState internally but shipped without a "use client" directive, so rendering it from the Server-Component landing page threw 'useState is not a function' at build time. Fixed at the component itself (the correct architectural fix, not a page-level workaround); the rest of the DS components were checked and none other uses hooks internally.

nodes.label: Gotcha: force-dynamic for DB-backed public pages
nodes.rationale: The landing page initially built as a static route, which would have baked in whatever the backend returned at BUILD time rather than serving live services. export const dynamic = "force-dynamic" makes it server-rendered on demand.

nodes.label: Gotcha: toLocaleDateString(undefined) uses the OS locale
nodes.rationale: Month/date labels rendered in Arabic ('يوليو 2026') on the test machine even though no i18n was wired up. Always pass an explicit locale ('en-US') until real i18n exists. Caught via an actual browser snapshot, not assumed.

nodes.label: Gotcha: avoid native number/date/time inputs (OS locale digits)
nodes.rationale: Chromium renders <input type=number|date|time> using the OS locale — on an Arabic-locale machine this produced Arabic-Indic digits ('٣٠') and Arabic day/month/hour labels in the native picker. Treated as a real fix rather than a cosmetic footnote given the project's explicit RTL/Arabic plans: replaced with type=text plus format placeholders (YYYY-MM-DD, HH:MM) and regex validation, so value/change events stay plain strings. This choice was later a deliberate, flagged deviation from the literal Claude Design mockups, which used native pickers.

nodes.label: lib/api.ts fetch wrapper (empty-body safe)
nodes.rationale: Injects the Bearer token and checks response text before JSON.parse regardless of status code — not just for 204 — so a 200 with an empty body (e.g. from a void controller method) cannot throw.

nodes.label: M0 — Project scaffold, git init, first push
nodes.rationale: Monorepo app/backend + app/frontend under one repo. Root .gitignore deliberately excluded notebook.txt (its own header says it is not meant for LLM usage) and .claude/settings.local.json (machine-local permissions), plus .idea/. Verified nothing sensitive was staged before the first commit.

nodes.label: M1 — JPA entities & repositories
nodes.rationale: All 8 entities + enums + Spring Data repositories built to match V1__init_schema.sql exactly. Booting against the live schema is what exposed the silently-non-running Flyway — the milestone was declared complete only after real verification, not claimed.

nodes.label: M2 — Auth + JWT security
nodes.rationale: Backend security/config/auth packages plus /sign-in and /sign-up pages with redirect-back via ?redirect= (FR-2). Three real bugs found by live testing rather than review: jjwt API drift, the Jackson 3 relocation, and the /api/auth/** over-permit.

nodes.label: M3 — Service browsing + landing page
nodes.rationale: Public GET /api/services (+/{id}), landing page and /book grid with an auth-aware Book button. A false positive during browser testing (Book going straight to /book/3) turned out to be a leftover JWT in localStorage from M2 testing — cleared and retested to confirm the real logged-out gate.

nodes.label: M4 — Core booking journey
nodes.rationale: Month/day availability endpoints, a public booking-window endpoint so the frontend never trusts the client clock, AppSettingsCache, and the transactional POST /api/bookings. The frontend shipped a month-dropdown instead of the spec'd year-picker + 12-month grid — called out explicitly as a scope simplification with the same functional guarantee, not silently substituted. Demo provider bcrypt hashes were extracted from real registrations through the app's own /api/auth/register so they are guaranteed encoder-compatible, never hand-computed.

nodes.label: M5 — Dashboard + management CRUD
nodes.rationale: All endpoints role-guarded via @PreAuthorize: appointments list with filters, availability bulk-generate/list/delete, service CRUD + provider assignment, user CRUD + promote (self-delete blocked, delete-with-dependencies → 409), and the admin booking-window PUT that refreshes the cache. Seeding a demo admin was a bootstrapping requirement since only an admin can create users and none existed. Four real bugs surfaced here, all via live curl + browser rather than review.

nodes.label: M6 — Integrations (Google Meet + email)
nodes.rationale: Verified up to the manual Google-consent boundary: the real 'click Allow' step needs the user's own Google identity and was deliberately left manual (same boundary as the Cloud Console setup), while everything on both sides of it was tested — authorize URL shape, callback error paths, the not-bookable gate, and a full booking against a fallback-link provider with real Gmail credentials.

nodes.label: M6.3 — Claude Design fidelity pass (six phases)
nodes.rationale: Source of truth was the ACTUAL Claude Design projects fetched via the DesignSync MCP (get_project/list_files/get_file) — grounded, not guessed. Four clarifying questions were asked up front before any code. Six phases each browser-verified and committed separately: landing/services fidelity, booking calendar (incl. a new 'full' day-cell bucket so fully-booked days keep their 0/N badge and stay clickable instead of looking empty), bulk generator rebuild with a live preview endpoint, status-lifecycle backend, status-lifecycle frontend, and the dashboard rebuild.

nodes.label: Verification discipline: curl matrix + chrome-devtools browser walkthrough
nodes.rationale: Every milestone was verified against running systems rather than claimed complete. Two layers: a curl matrix covering happy AND error/denial paths (RBAC denials, privilege escalation, idempotency, cross-provider ownership, advance-limit math), then a real browser walkthrough via the chrome-devtools MCP with the console checked for errors. Multiple bugs — the Arabic-locale inputs, the 200-vs-204 delete, the stale provider collection — were only findable this way; none would have survived to production, and none were caught by code review.

nodes.label: context7 MCP (up-to-date library docs)
nodes.rationale: Used before writing code against any library so the output matches current APIs rather than training data — verified Google Calendar Maven coordinates, the Flyway 10 separate-postgres-module fact, spring-dotenv's version against its CHANGELOG, and the Spring Boot 4.1.0 source for the Flyway autoconfig move. Honest limit recorded: for jjwt 0.13.0 even context7's indexed snippet was stale, so live IDE diagnostics were the real catch.

nodes.label: Gotcha: Claude Desktop skills are not visible to Claude Code
nodes.rationale: The drawio skill uploaded via the Claude Desktop app was unreachable from the Claude Code VSCode extension — they use separate skill registries (~/.claude/skills/ + plugins vs the desktop uploaded-skills store). Worked around by authoring the .drawio XML directly (draw.io is plain XML), which produced the same editable result.

nodes.label: Vercel deployment flow (CLI-driven)
nodes.rationale: Real journey recovered by parsing the session .jsonl since the history had only scattered mentions: split-stack deploy (Vercel frontend + Render backend/Postgres); CLI installed but not logged in; vercel login needs an interactive browser confirmation Claude CANNOT complete, so Claude runs it and hands over the URL/code; then vercel link (creates .vercel, git-ignored) → set Root Directory → vercel env add → vercel --prod; afterwards update APP_CORS_ORIGINS and the Google redirect URI to the real URL. Five obstacles were extracted and pre-smoothed for trainees.

nodes.label: Vercel MCP (deploy management + logs)
nodes.rationale: Verified from the docs, not memory: https://mcp.vercel.com is a hosted OAuth remote MCP and Claude Code is an officially supported client. It manages projects/deployments, reads deploy logs to diagnose failures accurately, and searches docs — but has NO environment-variable tools, so env vars and the actual deploy stay on the CLI. Decision: MCP + CLI hybrid, MCP connected as a one-time prerequisite. The original booking run was all-CLI simply because no Vercel MCP was connected then.

nodes.label: Supabase MCP
nodes.rationale: Added because the default trainee stack needs Supabase login working on Day 1. Verified against the official Supabase docs as an OAuth flow with NO personal access token — explicitly correcting the user-supplied YouTube-derived walkthrough, which described a PAT-based flow. Scoped --scope project since the database belongs to one project only.

nodes.label: bootcamp_roadmap_and_curriculum.md (Arabic curriculum)
nodes.rationale: Entirely in Arabic, numbered from 1, built iteratively behind review gates. Audience is near-beginner (barely aware frontend/backend/hosting exist), so even tokens and Pro usage limits are taught. Per-section pattern X.1 concept · X.2 steps · X.3 trainer impl+review · X.4 trainee impl+review · X.5 Q&A, with all booking-project specifics confined to collapsible «ما كتبه المدرب» blocks so the generic steps stay product-agnostic. Grew from a 6-day to a 10-day / 40h program.

nodes.label: Rule: ground curriculum sections in sources, never memory
nodes.rationale: Added to CLAUDE.md §A.5 after repeated writing-from-memory errors — including a fabricated example claiming the trainer 'rejected provider-first browsing' when that was actually the assistant's own scope analysis. Every curriculum section must re-read the booking-system part of conversation_history.md plus PROJECT_REPORT.md and extract the real decisions, order and gotchas. Paired rule: never NAME internal/graded docs inside the trainee-facing curriculum — they are extraction sources only.

nodes.label: Collaboration principle: trainee gives notes, Claude formats
nodes.rationale: Promoted to a first-class golden rule after the SRS section was found to contradict the bootcamp's premise: it asked trainees to hand-author EARS/user-story/Gherkin, which is a software engineer's job and is NOT what the trainer actually did — he wrote informal notes and asked Claude to format them. The loop is: trainee provides free-form notes → Claude researches and SUGGESTS the formal artifact → trainee reviews → repeat. The concept is still taught so the trainee can review intelligently; only the authoring burden is removed.

nodes.label: Principle: the trainee never reads or writes code
nodes.rationale: Every 'review the generated code' instruction was purged from the curriculum and both rule files. The trainee reviews by USING the product's UI and by reading Claude's plain-language report — never by reading code. Consequence: verification steps that can't be done through the UI (confirming password hashing, confirming keys are out of the code) were reworded to 'ask Claude to show evidence in its report'. Also drove the .env fix: the trainee pastes keys into chat and Claude writes the file, since hand-editing .env is the reliably-breaking step for non-technical people and was the one place the model was violated.

nodes.label: Three-layer testing owned by Claude
nodes.rationale: Whenever anything is built, Claude automatically (1) writes re-runnable automated test cases per functionality, (2) exercises the server from the command line, (3) drives the real browser via chrome-devtools — then reports in non-technical language. The trainee merely triggers it, even implicitly, since any development entails its testing; their own testing is using the UI. Honesty flag recorded: the booking project itself has only the default scaffold test, so the automated-test layer was documented as a forward-looking recommendation and NOT falsely claimed in the trainer example.

nodes.label: Rule: every plan opens with a plain-language summary
nodes.rationale: Plan-mode output is full of technical terms the trainee cannot review. Every implementation plan must open with a jargon-free «ماذا سنبني الآن؟» / 'What we'll build now' block of 3–6 bullets — the only part the trainee reads and approves — with all technical detail after it under a clearly-labelled 'need not read' heading.

nodes.label: Rule: passwords always hashed
nodes.rationale: Made explicit rather than assumed: Claude always stores passwords hashed, never plaintext, and the trainer's only job is to verify they actually are — via Claude's report, not by opening files.

nodes.label: Rule: Claude starts and explicitly stops test servers
nodes.rationale: Born from a real incident: a test instance left running on port 8080 from an earlier turn served a mysterious /login page that confused the user into thinking the backend had code it didn't have. Claude must stop what it starts so the trainee never hits a 'port occupied' error.

nodes.label: Default trainee stack: full-stack Next.js + Supabase + Vercel
nodes.rationale: One full-stack Next.js (TS) app in a single app/ folder with NO frontend/backend split — that split is only needed when the two halves are different languages, as in the booking project. Supabase chosen over Neon because it adds built-in auth, which makes sign-up/sign-in much easier for beginners. Deploy to Vercel with the DB already hosted → one deploy, all free tiers, and dev == prod so nothing drifts. SQLite was considered and rejected: zero setup, but it doesn't deploy cleanly on serverless. Asking beginners to install Docker Desktop just to run Postgres was judged overkill. The trainee's manual work is accounts and keys only; scaffolding, DB wiring and design components are Claude's job.

nodes.label: project-package/ (trainee handoff package)
nodes.rationale: Everything a trainee needs consolidated into one copyable folder: CLAUDE.md, PRODUCT.md, the curriculum (.md + .docx), and .claude/rules + .claude/skills. Files were moved with git mv so history is preserved for blame/log --follow. The .ar suffixes were dropped on the move since the whole package is Arabic by definition.

nodes.label: Four-surface package contract
nodes.rationale: Written to stop duplication recurring: each file answers exactly ONE question. CLAUDE.md = who am I / where are we / what do I read next (loaded every message). rules/*.md = how do I behave always (loaded in full every message, so keep short). skills/<name>/SKILL.md = how do I execute this section (description only in context, body on demand). curriculum + PRODUCT.md = the only two files the TRAINEE reads. Deliberate exception: template prompts live in BOTH the skill and the trainee-facing material — belt and braces — and a note forbids a future pass from 'helpfully' deduplicating them.

nodes.label: Discovery: skills lazy-load, rules do not
nodes.rationale: Confirmed against the official memory docs: rules without a paths: field load unconditionally at CLAUDE.md priority, and @import does not help because imported files still enter the context window at launch. The package was costing ~34KB of context every turn before the trainee typed a word — on a Pro plan whose 5-hour limit the curriculum itself warns about. Skills are the native lazy-loading mechanism (only the description sits in context). A hand-rolled playbooks.md proposal was withdrawn for reinventing this worse; paths:-scoped rules were rejected as the primary mechanism due to open bugs and used only for i18n, where the worst case degrades to current behaviour. Result: ~20KB per message, and it stays flat as new playbooks are added.

nodes.label: PRODUCT.md (per-trainee product state)
nodes.rationale: Created so the curriculum's fill-in blanks become read-only templates and the trainee's real answers live in one clean file. Critical constraint: this keeps the roadmap file IDENTICAL for every trainee, which is mandatory once it becomes the presentation deck's source. Written by Claude from free-form trainee input and rewritten in place — it holds current state, never a log.

nodes.label: Day-1 bootstrap (assistant identity protocol)
nodes.rationale: On ANY opening message ('السلام عليكم', «انت مين») Claude introduces itself as the bootcamp assistant, determines the current day and starts guiding without waiting to be asked. Day detection order: the progress ledger, then which of PRODUCT.md / conversation_history.md / app code exist, then — package files only → Day 1 fresh start. It reads only §6.N for that day, never the whole 164KB roadmap. Ongoing, Claude proposes the next step but the trainee may redirect; when asked for something out of sequence Claude names what is pending and says whether it is a real prerequisite.

nodes.label: Rule: pasted API keys are never echoed or logged
nodes.rationale: A pasted key is used in the command or written to .env only — never echoed back, never written to conversation_history.md or PRODUCT.md; log '<تم استلام المفتاح>' instead. Without this rule the 'log every prompt and response' protocol would have captured the trainee's key verbatim in a committed file.

nodes.label: MCP setup: what Claude can and cannot do
nodes.rationale: Verified by running claude mcp --help in-session rather than assuming. Claude CAN run claude mcp add itself, detect the OS and pick shell/quoting, and verify with claude mcp list. Claude CANNOT complete /mcp → Authenticate, an interactive TUI needing the trainee's browser identity. Critical warning: a newly added server is NOT live in the current session, so Claude must tell the trainee to restart or they will think the setup failed.

nodes.label: Independent QA agent timing analysis
nodes.rationale: Run with cold-start context deliberately to avoid biased results, and given three hypotheses to TEST rather than assume. Estimated 2,382 minutes against a 2,150-minute container (+232). Verdicts: 'days 1–5 too light' was PARTLY FALSE and misdiagnosed (Day 5 is the second-most overloaded day); 'days 6–10 overloaded' TRUE and strongly (Day 6 asks 176 min of work into an 80-min slot); 'hands-on from day one' TRUE as a goal and violated — nothing runs before Day 6 and the first live URL is Day 10 with zero recovery time. Root cause: §6 gave every content section a full day's four slots regardless of its actual weight — the schedule was built by dividing sections across days, not by estimating work. The agent flagged its own estimates as analytic not observed, with relative ordering far more reliable than absolute minutes, and recommended piloting Day 6 with two real beginners as the sharpest calibration test.

nodes.label: Option A-1: scaffold Day 1, first deploy Day 3
nodes.rationale: Rests on one technical fact: the initial scaffold depends on NO document, so with a fixed stack Claude can stand up a running authenticated app from 'my product is about X'. Chosen over A-2 (early scaffold, late deploy) and A-3 (cut only). Fixes the Day-10 cliff — the single biggest risk to the bootcamp's headline promise — makes redeploying routine, and dissolves the DesignSync ordering bug because the repo now exists from Day 1. Accepted risks: Day 1 becomes the new pressure point (a first-day failure is psychologically worse than a day-six one) and a shell built Day 1 may feel like thrown-away work — framed as 'Day 1 builds the empty house, Day 6 furnishes it'. The trainer explicitly REJECTED the proposed 'hand a stuck trainee the trainer's demo repo' mitigation.

nodes.label: Defect: DesignSync ran against a repo that didn't exist yet
nodes.rationale: The design section told trainees to pull components into 'your project repo' on Day 5, but the repo didn't exist until Day 6 — and the pull was duplicated again in the build section. Resolved by making the design section design-ONLY (visually generate and review, nothing pulled) and having each per-functionality build iteration run /design-sync for that iteration's specific piece.

nodes.label: Decision: per-iteration testing vs final integration pass
nodes.rationale: Three models were offered and the user picked (a): the build section asks 'does this piece work alone' via per-iteration testing that already exists in its stage rhythm, while the testing section becomes a FINAL cross-functionality pass asking 'does everything still work together' — multi-step scenarios across functionalities (book → cancel → confirm the slot reopens) plus a whole-app security sweep. This resolved the open question of how to span the iteration concept across days without duplicating it.

nodes.label: Curriculum renumbering and reordering passes
nodes.rationale: Done with scripted regex passes plus physical block reassembly rather than 100+ manual edits, then swept for inline cross-references that don't auto-update (bold task links, 'القسم N' prose, bare self-references). Two real traps: a first pass missed all 40 #### headers because the regex only covered ##/###, leaving them one level below their parent; and folding one section into another resolved an anchor collision where two different subsections slugged identically. Anchors were validated programmatically by reimplementing github-slugger's rules — 105 links, 0 broken — after an initial checker produced false positives by mishandling the Arabic ؟ (U+061F), which sits in the Arabic Unicode block but is stripped by the slugger.

nodes.label: DOCX RTL fix: run-level w:rtl, not just paragraph bidi
nodes.rationale: The first export came out entirely LTR with English collapsing into Arabic and a million false spelling squiggles, because direction was set only at the paragraph level (<w:bidi/>). Regenerated with run-level <w:rtl/> on all 1700 Arabic runs, code/inline-code kept LTR, section-level bidi injected into sectPr via a safe zip rewrite, RTL TOC styles, and correct proofing language (w:bidi=ar-SA on Arabic, en-US on Latin) — which is what actually removes the false squiggles. Built via the docx skill's docx-js path since pandoc/LibreOffice were absent, so no visual proof could be rendered.

nodes.label: Decision: presentation deck = single self-contained HTML, dual-mode
nodes.rationale: Dual-mode (عرض / مرجع): concepts render as projector slides, steps render as a searchable document with copy buttons. Chosen because it is RTL-native, works offline, preserves code blocks and links, and regenerates in one pass from the roadmap file. Rejected: PowerPoint (lossy regeneration, poor RTL), Google Slides (weakest RTL, needs internet), PDF (rigid — can't hold fill-in blanks). Deferred until §7–§17 content stops moving; the roadmap file stays the master source that generates it.

nodes.label: Arabic EARS/Gherkin/journey keywords
nodes.rationale: The user asked why translatable English keywords (WHEN, WHILE, IF, THEN, Given) survived in an Arabic file. Translated to عندما/أثناء/إذا…فعندئذٍ and بافتراض/عندما/فإنّ, keeping only the standard names EARS/Gherkin. The same treatment was later applied to the JOURNEY/ACTOR/START/DECISION/IF/END format keywords → الرحلة/الفاعل/البداية/قرار/إذا/النهاية.

nodes.label: JOURNEY/DECISION user-journey text format
nodes.rationale: A structured text shape (JOURNEY / ACTOR / numbered steps / DECISION with IF … -> go to step / END) defined up front specifically so the Day-1 prose journey converts cleanly into a Day-2 activity diagram without ambiguity. Claude reformats the trainee's raw description into it without dropping any step.

nodes.label: SRS: FR-1…FR-16 and NFR-1…NFR-6
nodes.rationale: Grew iteratively rather than being authored once: FR-1…12 initially (incl. FR-10 dashboard, FR-11 admin provider filter, FR-12 explicit RBAC-deny), then FR-13 per-provider Google, FR-14/15 booking horizon + calendar limits, FR-16 consumer-only self-registration. Later restructured so each requirement is self-contained (EARS base + user story + Gherkin + Main?/Priority together) with the tables reduced to an ID+title index — because scattering a requirement's parts across tables made it unreadable.

nodes.label: Scope discipline: service-first journey, no provider filter
nodes.rationale: A provider filter on the services grid was declined on two grounds: the journey is service-first (pick service → pick date → THEN providers surface as dropdowns, since relevance depends on the date), so a provider filter there would be a different undesigned entry point; and FR-1 only requires listing services publicly, making it new scope. Filtering was kept to a single client-side search box by service name — no backend query needed at this scale. Provider-first browsing was recorded as legitimate future work, not built.
